episodes.title: Johnny Bangorter's Rocky Mountain Militia: Helicopter Scare and Purgatory Jail
episodes.description:
One week inside the Rocky Mountain Militia in Leverkin, Utah. A low-flying helicopter, a court showdown, and a sheriff proud of his new Purgatory jail.

Led by Johnny Bangorter, the group swings from defiance to suspicion: no phones, one in the chamber, and constant scanning of skies and neighbors. Dave proudly displays a Mini-14 with a 40 round magazine as talk turns to whether the chopper overhead is federal surveillance. Barbara Bailey, quieter than most, explains how an old home video was used in court to label her dangerous, then waits for weekly calls from the children she can now only see under supervision. Mary Lynn readies for a New York talk show and an ultrasound, while her mother Mary braces for the culture shock.

Across town, the Washington County sheriff walks cameras through his new facility, determined to label the jail Purgatory and planning to arrest Johnny away from home after a heated traffic stop involving a constantly chambered handgun. Law enforcement tell the filmmakers they do not consider the group a serious threat, even as the militia revels in being named a notorious hate group.

Out on the desert rim they call the cracks above the Grand Canyon, training mixes with rhetoric about defending families at any cost. A new recruit says the militia helped him leave drugs behind. The crew becomes another node in the rumor mill as license plates are noted, vans parked tactically are logged, and trust thins with each pass of a chopper.

episodes.title: Father Antonio Felices and the Triangular UFO Over Valladolid, 1965
episodes.description:
A Dominican priest watched a giant triangular UFO over Valladolid in 1965, sparking a Church-wide debate on aliens, science, and faith. This episode follows the evidence.

On September 16, 1965, Father Antonio Felices and thousands across Valladolid, Trappa, Buesillo, and the Villanubla Aerodrome stared at a metallic triangle hanging in the afternoon sky. Through a telescope, Felices detailed its color as gunmetal bluing, noted a huge belly and fin-like edges, and saw smaller lights dart in and out as if from a mothership. Pilot El Yodoro Carrion was vectored to the object’s vertical and, from 23 km altitude, compared it against a passing airliner, estimating the craft at roughly three times the plane’s size. Analyst Javier Dominguez Hadoga reconstructs the scene, explaining why early size estimates ballooned while reinforcing key features many reported.

From Giordano Bruno and Galileo to today’s Vatican Observatory in Tucson, the film traces how the Church has wrestled with the UFO question. We hear how observatory researchers frame their mission as doing science, not seeking aliens to evangelize, and we speak with former director Jesuit Father José Gabriel Funes (2006-2015). Funes stresses that proof of extraterrestrial life must come from science, that interstellar travel is practically impossible with current technology and distances, and that the Church has no special protocol for contact. If discovery comes, he says, the Church would follow leading scientists, showing patience and humility while discussing astrobiology and exotheology in serious academic forums.

The story widens to other triangular encounters: Belgium’s 1990 radar-detected wave with F-16 scrambles and a close photograph; a Camino de Santiago pilgrim who described three bright vertices, eerie silence, a close approach, and 45 to 50 minutes of missing time; and a 1995 Lugo case at the Askandaras military magazine reportedly recorded in infrared. We also revisit priests drawn to these enigmas, from Salvador Freichedo’s provocative theses to Father Pedro Pablo Requejo’s participation in a 1980s contact group that reported timed formations over Mugardos’ Chancillas beach.

EXtraterrestrials: They are Among Us asks what confirmed nonhuman intelligence would mean for doctrine, evangelization, and the faithful - and how the Curia might respond as governments and militaries grow more open.

episodes.title: Taiwan's First Same-Sex Buddhist Temple Wedding - Bhikkhunis Lead the Change
episodes.description:
A historic same sex Buddhist temple wedding in Taiwan opens a wider look at women's ordination and equality across Asia.

In The Buddha Code, we follow the Dharma's 2,500-year journey from India across Central and East Asia to the Himalayas and Southeast Asia, asking how the teachings were safeguarded and lived. Today, those scriptures and precepts guide more than a billion Buddhists, and they frame a timely question: who gets to walk this path, and on what terms?

At the heart is the love and resolve of Mei Yu and Yating Yu, who choose a Buddhist ceremony and become Taiwan's first same-gender couple married in a Buddhist temple. Their wedding at Buddhist Tongxi College in Taoyuan City drew national attention as society debated 2018 referendum questions on marriage equality and civil rights.

We also meet Venerable Chao Hui, who champions equality within Taiwanese Buddhism, and Theravada bhikkhunis Venerable Damananda (Thailand) and Venerable Ketumala (Myanmar), who describe legal barriers at home, the Sri Lankan lineage that confers ordination, and international leadership training to build capacity. Despite obstacles, women's ordinations are growing.

Taiwan offers a contrasting model. Democratic freedoms and broad access to education have allowed bhikkhunis to flourish alongside bhikkhus and lay practitioners. At Luminary Buddhist Institute in Chiayi, days begin at 4:30 am with recitation and mindfulness. Trainees keep daily reflection diaries, study the Dhammapada with modern psychology, science, and technology, and learn teamwork before serving in Kaohsiung Dhamma centers and city communities.

Socially engaged Buddhism appears in the work of Venerable Yian Wan of Fangsheng Temple, which welcomes all Buddhist schools. He supports an indigenous Taiwanese tribe with fair crop purchases, school and sports donations, and a volunteer medical clinic for elders and families.

Rooted in the teaching that liberation does not depend on gender, this episode shows bhikkhunis leading temples, education, and service. Mei Yu and Yating Yu's vows embody a living Dharma for a diverse, modern world.

episodes.title: Freemasons: Oxford's Apollo Lodge and the First Football Lodge Consecration
episodes.description:
With rare access, we step inside modern English Freemasonry at Oxford's Apollo Lodge and the birth of the first football lodge, culminating in the Grand Investiture.

As the United Grand Lodge of England marks 300 years, cameras are invited to reveal rituals, regalia, fellowship and charity at the heart of the craft. We see the strain of declining membership as Assistant Grand Secretary Tony Rayner closes historic lodges, even handling a warrant signed when the future Edward VII was Grand Master. With only 2% of members under 30 and nearly 100 lodges closing each year, the fraternity rallies to modernize without losing tradition.

On campus at Oxford’s Apollo University Lodge, Dr David Staples helps spearhead the University Scheme. In a lodge once associated with Oscar Wilde and Cecil Rhodes, students don black or white tie, officers in court dress, and candidates are quietly prepared out of view. Staples explains how shorter, livelier meetings and clear expectations make initiation relevant to undergraduates while preserving ancient ritual.

In Leicester, Professor Andy Green welcomes prospective members, breaking down subscriptions, dining costs and charitable giving. He speaks candidly about chronic fatigue syndrome and how the brotherhood’s support helped him through dark days, underscoring Freemasonry’s promise of personal growth, stability and camaraderie beyond work and home.

To reach new audiences, UGLE backs special-interest lodges. We follow David Lallana and Sean Whelan as they consecrate Football Lodge No. 9921, complete with football-boot gavels, a bespoke emblem and a rousing club-style song. In a solemn ceremony led by the Provincial Grand Master, corn, wine and oil are scattered to bless the new lodge as Lallana takes the chair as Primus Master before 250 brethren.

The year crescendos at Freemasons' Hall, London, where 1,800 gather for Annual Investiture. HRH The Duke of Kent presides as 373 brethren receive grand rank. James Long moves from Grand Sword Bearer to Deputy President of the Board, while Dr David Staples is invested as Deputy Grand Director of Ceremonies after a nerve-testing rehearsal he’s determined not to fumble.

This chapter of Inside the Freemasons pulls back the curtain on myth and mystery to show why ritual, service and brotherhood still matter in a 300-year-old craft adapting for the future.

episodes.title: Gabriel's Inscription: Was Simon of Perea the Messiah Before Jesus?
episodes.description:
A 2,000-year-old inked stone tablet may upend what we think we know about the Messiah.

Investigative filmmaker Simcha Jacobovici follows the trail of the mysterious “Gabriel’s Inscription” — a Hebrew text that reads “Gabriel, I command you… in three days live.” Is this a third-day resurrection tied not to Jesus, but to an earlier messianic leader? From the Church of the Holy Sepulchre to the Dead Sea’s desert fortresses, we examine parallels with the Dead Sea Scrolls, why the letters hang from ruled lines, and why the text was painted rather than carved. With Professor Israel Noll and epigrapher Robert Deutsch, the story points to Perea, an illicit antiquities pipeline, a Swiss collector, and one explosive candidate: Simon of Perea. Three “shepherds,” a ravine, a body denied burial, and a radical idea of a suffering messiah emerge — but the crucial links are not where you expect.

episodes.title: Freemasons at Chelsea Lodge: Beatboxer’s Second Degree and the Music Lodge
episodes.description:
Cameras go inside Chelsea Lodge as a beatboxer takes his Second Degree, and a new Music Lodge is born in Cardiff. Freemasonry opens its doors inside UGLE.

Marking 300 years of the United Grand Lodge of England in central London, this episode lifts the veil on regalia, ceremonies and the little plays that masons call ritual, tackling the jokes about funny handshakes and rolled up trouser legs head on. Sir David Wooten addresses online conspiracy myths and recalls how visibility changed after World War II, when up to 200,000 Freemasons were murdered under Nazi occupation and lodges went low profile. Today there are around 200,000 members in England and Wales, who must believe in a supreme being of their own choice, and devil worship is forbidden.

In Bedfordshire, Dean’s Russell Lodge prepares a traditional Ladies’ Night. His wife Mitch, named first lady for the evening, battles nerves and finally delivers a witty rhyming thank you, revealing the social traditions and tensions of a craft that many still describe as a big boys’ club.

At London’s Chelsea Lodge, worshipful master Chas Elliott leads a troupe of showbiz masons. With Roger De Corcy and Nookie Bear among the brethren and 70s prog rocker Rick Wakeman in attendance, rehearsals are treated like a production. In front of more than 200 visitors, rapper and beatbox artist Jonathan Chandrupandi, formerly the world’s fastest rapper, answers the classic “sun at its meridian” test and nails his Second Degree before a cabaret-style Festive Board.

In South Wales, undertaker Matthew Sims, who received help from the Royal Masonic Trust for Girls and Boys to complete his master’s degree, founds a new Music Lodge with Provincial Grand Director of Ceremonies Peter Jones. Their meticulously staged consecration flows to perfection, ending in well-earned gin and tonics and a song. Along the way, leaders rebut the “backscratching” myth, stressing strict rules against using the craft for business and highlighting how Masonic charities support members and families.

After a two-hour ceremony he emerges a second degree mason, discovering the journey is less about pecuniary gain and more about discipline, study and self-improvement.

At the Friendship Lodge, worshipful master Gary Southam commits pages of ritual to memory. When a candidate stumbles during the Q&A, Gary reflects on why masonry asks men to put in the work and live by its teachings beyond the lodge.

Charity runs throughout. In the basement of Freemasons Hall we see the Masonic Charitable Foundation’s impact, with multi-million-pound grants aiding both masonic families and national causes like the Scouts and Air Ambulance.

In Rome, survivors knock on the doors of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in search of their records, while church experts including Vatican journalist Robert Mickens and Jesuit Father Hans Zollner discuss the cost of secrecy and the challenge of restoring trust. episodes.title: Freemasons: From William Morgan's 1826 Disappearance to Italy's P2 Scandal
episodes.description:
A veteran vanishes in 1826 and a banker is found hanged in 1982. This episode traces Freemasonry from William Morgan's disappearance to Italy's P2 scandal.

From medieval stone masons' guilds and the 1717 Grand Lodge of England to the secret oaths, Blue Lodge degrees, and symbols like the square, compass, and the letter G, we map how this fraternity grew across Britain, France, Germany, and the United States. We examine Andrew Michael Ramsey's Templar-flavored origin story, the Strict Observance rite, and Adam Weishaupt's Illuminati attempt to hijack it.

In Paris, we explore the Grand Orient de France, the Nine Sisters Lodge, and claims that Freemasons propelled the French Revolution, noting figures like the Duke of Orleans and Jacobin journalist Jacques René Hébert while separating evidence from propaganda. Across the Atlantic, we look at George Washington and other founders, recurring Masonic motifs in Washington DC, and why the order appealed to revolutionary-era leaders.

The turning point arrives in Batavia, New York. After announcing a tell-all, Captain William Morgan vanished in 1826 following an arrest for an alleged debt. With a body never found and trials involving Masonic officials, public outrage collapsed New York lodges from 480 to 82 in seven years, sparked the Anti-Masonic Party, and reshaped the Jackson vs. John Quincy Adams era. Of 54 men indicted, 11 were convicted on kidnapping charges; no one was convicted of murder.

We track Albert Pike's expansion of the Scottish Rite, his Confederate role, and his rejection of integration, alongside the rise of Prince Hall Freemasonry for Black Americans. We note how the KKK mimicked fraternal trappings while mainstream American Masonry later denounced the hate group.

Under Hitler, Göring declared there was no place for Freemasonry; lodges were dissolved and members were imprisoned in camps. Finally, we uncover Italy's clandestine Propaganda Due - P2 - under Licio Gelli, its ties to Banco Ambrosiano, the 1981 police raid that exposed a secret membership list including senior officials and Silvio Berlusconi, and the 1982 hanging of banker Roberto Calvi under Blackfriars Bridge before the Grand Orient of Italy abolished P2.

From charity-minded Shriners to infamous scandals, this balanced history separates myth from record to understand how a house of many rooms shaped politics, cities, and culture.

episodes.description:

This Crime Stories episode follows the investigation into the murder of Alexandra Fossmo and the attempted murder of neighbor Daniel Linde within the tight-knit Philadelphia Church community. After a pre-dawn knock at his door, Daniel is shot in the mouth and chest yet manages to call for help. Moments later, friends discover Alexandra shot in her bed with no signs of forced entry. Forensics recover a .38 caliber bullet from a pillow and track a single set of small footprints through the snow to car tire marks, overturning the early belief that a large male suspect was responsible.

Police soon focus on former nanny Sara Svensson. Her father’s Volvo tread matches casts from the scene, and roadblock logs show she drove past officers after the shootings. Brought in the next day, Sara confesses, mapping where she discarded clothing, a homemade silencer, and footwear. She says she threw the gun from the Oland Bridge. Yet she insists she acted alone and offers a startling motive: instructions from God sent to her phone.

Cell tower data shows the S Phone repeatedly traveling in tandem with Pastor Helge Fossmo’s registered phone. When confronted, Sara is shattered and admits a secret affair with Helge. Wiretaps then reveal Helge is also romantically involved with Annette Linda, the estranged wife of victim Daniel Linde, suggesting a plan to remove both spouses.

A forensic breakthrough restores deleted SIM data from Sara’s phone. Among the recovered texts: “a time for killing and a time for healing” and a cryptic two-part directive interpreted as first killing Alexandra, then Daniel. In court, a sound reenactment inside the Fossmo house demonstrates gunshots would have been heard from the children’s room where Helge claimed he slept. The verdict: Sara Svensson is convicted of murder and attempted murder and committed to psychiatric care; Pastor Helge Fossmo is convicted of incitement to murder and attempted murder and sentenced to life in prison.

Our investigation connects Portugal’s Fatima to Spain’s Garabandal and Palmar de Troia, Tenerife’s Mount La Corona, and Argentina’s Cerro Uritorco, asking if yesterday’s angels might be today’s UFOs.

In Fatima, between May and October 1917, shepherd children Jacinta, Francisco and Lucia reported encounters culminating on October 13 in the famed Dance of the Sun. Testimonies also mention entities ascending into a cloud within a beam of light and earlier sightings of strange beings in 1915, blurring the line between Marian visions and close encounters.

Veteran researchers from the Third Phase group, including Jose Luis Respuelo, documented erratic fire spheres 6 to 8 meters wide that left scorched circles on the mountainside. One witness recalled asking the figure of Mary about a transparent bubble beside her; the reply: "that's what I came in."

In Andalusia’s Palmar de Troia (1968), a local UFO wave preceded four girls describing a luminous woman in dark, quilted clothing floating above a tree, while silhouettes appeared near the lentisk trees. On Tenerife’s Mount La Corona (1992), a seer’s alleged contact shifted from extraterrestrial to Marian before thousands gathered at Fuente de Pedro reported a half-meter luminous figure.

We revisit the National Network of Correspondents with Jose Ruescamentiel, which logged around 1,500 UFO cases across Spain, with no more than 3 percent resisting explanation—among them the goat herder who swore he saw a “flying washing machine” with someone inside. Across continents, sacred geographies repeat: menhirs aligned with Benyasagara and Pena Sagra, Tiwanaku’s enigmatic stone portal, the Dogon and Egyptians looking to Sirius, and Cerro Uritorco’s long history of lights that helped make Capilla del Monte an Argentine hotspot.

Guerrero chronicled Spain's late 60s and 70s UFO boom, from Madrid's Ballena Alegre basement meetings to the Umo case, where Umites allegedly sent letters detailing their planet, technology and even theology. He debated skeptics and believers, compiled press clippings, and corresponded with engineers, doctors, priests and more from around the world, some letters arriving from India and France, even in Esperanto.

His archive, revealed here by journalist and former student Cristina Martín Jiménez, spans tens of thousands of documents, thousands of books and hundreds of audio and videotapes, including field interviews and parapsychology courses. Beyond ufology, he explored telepathy, clairvoyance, partial hypnosis and Zenner card experiments, while witnesses also credit him with healings by the laying on of hands.

A standout case revisited in this episode is his own sighting on August 10, 1989 over La Vega near the village: a bright object about a quarter of a full moon, apparently stationary, emitting a beam as a smaller light detached from it like a mothership releasing a craft. Reported across western Andalusia and moving against the wind, it strengthened his conviction that visitors might already be among us.

episodes.title: I Was In A Cult For 10 Years: Here's How I Escaped (Cult Witness Full Length Documentary Film
episodes.description:
At the age of 19 Samuel Stefan, consumed by crisis, was drawn into a cult. It would be 10 years before he was able to escape.

Using a technique called ‘love-bombing’ cults prey on the vulnerable, recruiting new members with love and warmth. After a period of brain-washing, members are forbidden to leave, enslaved through psychological control, and in Samuel’s case, even violence. He was finally able to escape in the dead of night, persued by other members and seek help.

Cult Witness is an intelligent exploration of how cults attract and manipulate their followers, sharing the disturbing firsthand experiences of Cult Witness director Samuel Stefan and six others who have freed themselves from cults: Jill Mytton (The Exclusive Brethren), Jim Bergin and Judy Garvey (The Gentle Wind Project), Lea Saskia Laasner (The Janus Project), and Celeste Jones and Amoreena Winkler (The Children of God).

Analytical insights into the cult experience are provided by leadership expert Betty Sue Flowers; Benjamin Zablocki, chair of the Department of Sociology at Rutgers University; UCLA Professor Emeritus Bertram Raven, an expert on interpersonal influence and social power relationships; psychotherapist Miguel Perlado, who specializes in cult-related problems; and Urs Eschmann, a specialist in legal issues involving cults.

Cult Witness unravels the hidden world of cults; the hold they have on their victims, the reasons people form and fall prey to them and what takes place within..
